newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait again moves to finalise UK missile deal.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait again moves to finalise UK missile deal.

text.p: Kuwait has reactivated steps to finalise a controversial $150 million deal for British Aerospace Plc Sea Skua missiles, industry experts said on Monday.

"Some annexes to the deal are being signed," said one Western expert who closely follows the order. "They are now discussing some possible technical amendments to facilitate the fitting and change delivery schedules."

Kuwait intends to fit eight fast patrol boats ordered from France in 1995 in a $500 million deal with the surface-to-surface missiles. The first of the warships was rolled out by Constructions Mecaniques de Normandie (CMN) last February.
The deal has been at the centre of clashes for a couple of years between parliament and the government over defence spending, middlemen and alleged squandering of public funds.
The head of parliament's Protection of Public Funds Committee Adnan Abdul-Samad earlier told Reuters the government had informed the house that it had approved the Sea Skua deal.
Parliament started a two-month summer recess on July 30.
"The British were told in July the deal could be finalised in July or August...There is some movement these days," said a Western military expert.

Some MPs have questioned a decision to drop a cheaper French offer for MM-15 missiles made by Aerospatiale. Both missiles are not in service although an air-launched version of the Sea Skua was successfully fired during the 1991 Gulf War by British helicopters against Iraqi warships.

In another controversial Kuwaiti defence requirement, a military team has returned home from a one-week visit to China where it discussed further details to the possible purchase of tracked Chinese self-propelled howitzer guns, experts said.
They said no final deal was signed.

There has been no official word on the Chinese guns but sources said a Kuwaiti military committee had in May recommended the Chinese to equip one batallion with 18 howitzers, possibly worth $200 million, with an option for a second.
News of the purchase has triggered private British advice to drop the Chinese offer and strong criticism by U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns.

Washington still hopes Kuwait would buy its M109 A6 Paladin gun, which is also deployed with U.S. troops in Kuwait. The British are rallying hard for their Desert AS90 while South Africa offered its LIW 155mm G6, the only wheeled system in the race.
Kuwait has a $12 billion plan lasting from 1992-2004 to rebuild it military, devastated during the 1990-91 Iraqi occupation.
